spoken.OrchardCore.Localization.Build: Orchard Core dot Localization dot Build

chapters.title: JavaScript Localization in Orchard Core
chapters.subtitle: Translate the strings of your scripts with PO files

steps.text: Scripts that draw part of a page need labels in the language of the visitor. Orchard Core gives them strings from the same PO files as your C# code. In this video, we'll write a localizer, pass its strings to a script, and translate them.

chapters.title: Why scripts need a localizer
chapters.subtitle: A script can't call the string localizer

steps.text: Your C# code translates text with a string localizer that reads PO files. A script runs in the browser, where it can't call that localizer, but the interface it draws still needs translated labels.
IJSLocalizer connects the two. A localizer returns a dictionary for a group name, the view writes the dictionary into the page, and the script reads it from there.
A localizer is a class that implements IJSLocalizer. It injects the string localizer of its own type, and GetLocalizations receives the name of a group.

When the group is yours, return a dictionary: each key, such as AddPolicy, is the name the script reads, and each value is a string localizer call whose English text becomes the message ID. For any other group, return null.
Register the class in the Startup of your module with AddScoped. Any number of modules can register a localizer, and each one answers only the groups it owns.

chapters.title: Pass the strings to the script
chapters.subtitle: From the view to the page, and into the script

steps.text: In a Razor view, call GetJSLocalizations on the Orchard helper with a group name. It asks every registered localizer, and returns the merged dictionary, translated for the culture of the request.
Serialize the dictionary to JSON, and put it in a data attribute of the element your script works on. The strings arrive with the page.
In the script, find that element, parse the attribute once, and pass the dictionary to setTranslations.
Orchard Core's helper merges it into one shared object, which getTranslations returns anywhere in your app. A component reads a string by its key, such as AddPolicy, and shows the translated text.

chapters.title: Translate with PO files
chapters.subtitle: The same files as your C# code

steps.text: Translations are ordinary PO entries. The context is the full name of the localizer class, and the message ID is the English text from the string localizer call.
Put the file where Orchard Core looks for PO files: in a Localization folder of your module, of the site, or of a tenant. Restart the application after you edit one.

chapters.title: See it in the admin
chapters.subtitle: The CORS settings page in French

steps.text: The CORS settings page is drawn by a script. Its search box, its Add a policy button and its Default Policy badge are strings from the cors-admin group.
Request the page in French, and the same strings come from a PO file instead. Nothing in the script changes.
Open a policy, and its titles, hints and buttons are translated too. Each one is a key of the dictionary that the view passed to the script.

chapters.title: Groups and templates
chapters.subtitle: Several groups, and a template for translators

steps.text: A view can request several groups in one call. Each group is resolved in turn, a localizer that returns null is skipped, and when two entries share a key, the last one wins.

Translators work from a template. Add the OrchardCore.Localization.Build package to your project, and run its UpdateLocalizationCatalog target. It reads the string localizer calls in C# and Razor code, not your script files.
That's JavaScript localization: a localizer per module, a dictionary per group, and the same PO files for your scripts as for your C# code. Thanks for watching.
